answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: From Marie Curie’s autobiographical notes, where she defends her and Pierre’s choice not to profit from radium. This exact wording is Vincent Sheean’s translation in Eve Curie’s Madame Curie (1937), p. 336, which reads “Humanity certainly needs practical men…”. The 1923 English edition of Pierre Curie gives the same passage in different words.

source.heading: Where it comes from

docMeta.dd: Madame Curie: A Biography, by Eve Curie
Vincent Sheean (Literary Guild of America printing, New York, 1937; © Doubleday, Doran)
End of ch. XXIII, “America”, p. 336, quoting Marie Curie’s autobiographical notes
Marie Curie, “Autobiographical Notes,” in Pierre Curie (Macmillan, 1923), trans. Charlotte & Vernon Kellogg

source.excerpt:
A large number of my friends affirm, not without valid reasons, that if Pierre Curie and I had guaranteed our rights, we should have acquired the financial means necessary to the creation of a satisfactory radium institute, without encountering the obstacles which were a handicap to both of us, and which are still a handicap for me. Nevertheless, I am still convinced that we were right.

Humanity certainly needs practical men, who get the most out of their work, and, without forgetting the general good, safeguard their own interests. But humanity also needs dreamers, for whom the disinterested development of an enterprise is so captivating that it becomes impossible for them to devote their care to their own material profit.

Without the slightest doubt, these dreamers do not deserve wealth, because they do not desire it. Even so, a well-organized society should assure to such workers the efficient means of accomplishing their task, in a life freed from material care and freely consecrated to research.
trail: 1923. Marie Curie’s “Autobiographical Notes” are published in English in Pierre Curie (Macmillan, trans. Charlotte & Vernon Kellogg). The passage there reads: “Humanity, surely, needs practical men who make the best of their work for the sake of their own interests, without forgetting the general interest. But it also needs dreamers…” Project Gutenberg #69617 ↗

1937. Eve Curie’s biography Madame Curie, translated by Vincent Sheean, quotes the notes in the wording that now circulates: “Humanity certainly needs practical men, who get the most out of their work… But humanity also needs dreamers…” (p. 336). Internet Archive scan ↗

Today. Wikiquote lists the line under Marie Curie’s sourced quotes, but cites only a 2003 astrophysics textbook (Dopita & Sutherland, Astrophysics of the Diffuse Universe) and not either Curie book. Wikiquote: Marie Curie ↗
source.excerptNote: As printed in Eve Curie, Madame Curie, trans. Vincent Sheean (1937), p. 336. Eve Curie introduces the passage as coming from “some short autobiographical notes drawn up after her return from America.”

author.name: Marie Curie
author.heading: Marie Curie
author.bio: Marie Curie (born Maria Skłodowska) pioneered research on radioactivity and discovered polonium and radium. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, and the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences: physics in 1903 and chemistry in 1911. In 1923 she published Pierre Curie, a memoir of her husband, together with her own autobiographical notes.

misattribution.heading: What gets garbled
misattribution.intro: The attribution holds: Marie Curie did write this. What drifts is the wording, and the source people give for it.

context.heading: Why she wrote it
lead: Marie and Pierre Curie published their method for preparing radium and took out no patent. In the 1923 notes Curie writes that this gave up “a fortune”. Friends argued that patent money could have paid for the radium institute she had to fund by appeals, including the American campaign that bought her a gram of radium.

The “dreamers” paragraph is her answer. She does not regret the choice, but says a well-organized society owes such researchers the means to work. In the 1937 translation, that means a life “freed from material care and freely consecrated to research.”
context.pull: Nevertheless, I am still convinced that we were right.
